Respiratory Illness Outbreak Challenges Canada’s Transportation & Logistics Firms

An outbreak of a highly contagious respiratory illness has struck several sites within Canada’s Transportation & Logistics industry, leading to significant workforce absenteeism and operational strain across the sector. The outbreak, first identified last week at a major distribution hub in the Greater Toronto Area, has since been reported at additional warehouses, freight terminals, and trucking depots in Ontario and British Columbia.

According to industry organization the Canadian Transportation & Logistics Association (CTLA), more than 1,200 workers across at least 15 sites have tested positive or are in precautionary isolation as of Wednesday. “We are seeing clusters of cases at key transit points, which has required rapid adjustments to staffing and shift schedules,” said CTLA spokesperson Evelyn McEwan. “Firms are prioritizing worker safety, but the operational impact is undeniable.”

LogiBridge Solutions, a national freight operator, has temporarily closed two of its Toronto-area facilities for deep cleaning and to facilitate testing of all employees. “A significant portion of our workforce is currently unavailable,” said company president Martin Fournier. “We’re operating at reduced capacity as we implement health protocols and support our affected staff.”

Other logistics providers, including FleetStream and Pacific Crosshaul, have reported similar disruptions. A FleetStream manager noted, “We’ve had to reassign drivers and delay some scheduled shipments. Our main focus is on preventing further spread among our teams.”

Industry analysts warn that continued outbreaks could lead to further logistical challenges, particularly if the situation extends into the coming weeks. “The Transportation & Logistics industry is heavily dependent on its frontline workforce to manage freight flow and site operations,” observed Sarah Liu, an independent supply chain analyst. “When you see these kinds of absentee rates, there’s a knock-on effect on throughput and scheduling.”

The CTLA has recommended all member firms enhance on-site health measures, including increased sanitization, mask mandates, and rapid testing where possible. Some firms have introduced temporary staggered shifts and remote work for administrative staff in an effort to limit site density.

Union representatives have called for hazard pay and additional paid sick leave for affected workers. “Our members are critical to keeping goods moving. Their health must come first,” said Teamsters Local 992 president Joel Lapointe.

With the outbreak still evolving, industry leaders are monitoring the situation closely and preparing further contingency plans to maintain critical operations.
